title: У Києві після атаки на Південний міст екстрено змінюють рух транспорту: нові маршрути і де додадуть автобуси
content_c:
У Києві після атаки на Південний міст екстрено змінюють рух транспорту: нові маршрути і де додадуть автобуси
У Києві тимчасово призупинили рух ділянкою «зеленої» лінії метро та перекрили Південний міст, через що столична влада пустила додаткові автобуси через Дарницький міст та посилила маршрут №1-М.
У Києві посилюють роботу наземного громадського транспорту через зміни в роботі метро.
Про це повідомляє КМДА у Telegram.
Посилення роботи наземного транспорту
У зв’язку зі збільшенням навантаження на «червону» лінію метрополітену на тимчасовому автобусному маршруті №1-М працюватимуть 15 одиниць рухомого складу.
Також через перекриття Південного мосту змінюється рух автобусів №№ 22, 91. Для забезпечення перевезення пасажирів рух цих маршрутів організовують через Дарницький міст.
На маршруті № 22 кількість автобусів збільшать на 4 одиниці — загалом працюватимуть 14 автобусів. Водночас 5 автобусів курсуватимуть на короткому відрізку вул. Тростянецька — ст. м. «Либідська».
На маршруті № 91 також додадуть 4 автобуси — загалом працюватимуть 7 одиниць рухомого складу.
«Просимо пасажирів із розумінням поставитися до ситуації, завчасно планувати свої маршрути та стежити за оперативними змінами в роботі громадського транспорту на офіційних інформаційних ресурсах», — зазначили у КМДА.
Зміни в роботі метрополітену
"Червона» лінія: рух поїздів здійснюється між станціями «Академмістечко» — «Лісова». Всі станції, зокрема «Чернігівська» та «Лісова», відкриті для пасажирів.
«Зелена» лінія: рух поїздів — між станціями «Сирець» — «Видубичі». Водночас рух поїздів між станціями «Осокорки» — «Червоний хутір» тимчасово призупинений.
У разі оголошення повітряної тривоги всі підземні станції працюють як укриття.
На місці працюють всі необхідні фахівці.
Про відновлення руху у звичайному режимі у Київському метрополітені повідомлять додатково.
Всі станції метро на червоній гілці відкриті для пасажирів. Рух поїздів здійснюється між станціями «Академмістечко» — «Лісова».
Пізно ввечері внаслідок атаки ворога були пошкодження між станціями «Дарниця» і «Чернігівська» та виходів зі станції «Лісова». Фахівці метрополітену працювали всю ніч, щоб забезпечити рух усіма станціями.
Піденний міст перекритий
За інформацією Патрульної поліції Києва, рух транспорту Південним мостом тимчасово перекритий.
Водіям варто враховувати цю інформацію під час планування поїздок.
Нагадаємо, ворог в ніч проти 27 жовтня атакував транспортну інфраструктуру столиці.
Мер Києва Віталій Кличко уточнив, що під час обстрілу столиці ворог влучив у Південний міст, в результаті чого було пошкоджено наземну інфраструктуру метрополітену.
Раніше повідомлялося, що у ніч проти 27 жовтня російські війська атакували Київ балістичними ракетами.

title: В Минцифры РФ советуют прятать дата-центры под землю из-за атак украинских дронов — СМИ
content_c:
Министерство цифрового развития России утвердило рекомендации по защите центров обработки данных от атак украинских беспилотников. Документ предусматривает создание резервных копий данных, сотрудничество бизнеса с силовыми структурами и физическую защиту объектов, в частности их размещение в подземных сооружениях, сообщает The Moscow Times со ссылкой на «Коммерсант».
Отмечается, что для наиболее важных центров обработки данных предлагается строить подземные помещения и использовать несколько уровней защиты, в частности системы радиоэлектронной борьбы. Также рекомендуется устанавливать сверхпрочные конструкции, способные выдержать ударную волну, и постоянно координировать работу ИТ-компаний с силовыми структурами, в частности с Росгвардией и Вооружёнными силами РФ.
В зависимости от важности, центры обработки данных разделили на три категории — «К1», «К2» и «К3». Для каждой из них предусмотрены отдельные требования к безопасности.
В частности, к самой высокой категории «К1» отнесли стратегические объекты, повреждение которых может нарушить работу государственных служб. Категория «К2» охватывает важные центры обработки данных регионального или отраслевого уровня. К «К3» отнесли корпоративные центры, повреждение которых не будет иметь критических последствий для государства в целом.
Издание пишет, что новые требования к защите центров обработки данных коснутся как государственных учреждений, так и частных компаний. Расходы на дополнительную безопасность могут привести к росту тарифов российских интернет-провайдеров на 10%.
Старший инвестиционный директор группы KAMA FLOW Роман Чустузиан отметил, что даже если укрытия, защитные сетки, датчики и резервные каналы связи увеличат стоимость объекта на 5–10%, эти расходы будут значительно меньше возможных убытков. По его словам, в случае повреждения центр может потерять 87% своей стоимости и прекратить работу на несколько месяцев.
Напомним, в сентябре российские атаки вывели из строя несколько дата-центров в Киеве. Среди них — «Парковый», «Омега Телеком» и центр обработки данных телекоммуникационного оператора Cosmonova.net. Все они в результате атак прекратили работу и перенесли свою деятельность на серверы в Европе.
Между тем недавние атаки украинских беспилотников на российские дата-центры, в частности на крупнейшее хранилище данных Сбербанка, три сервера компании Yandex и центр обработки данных «ВКонтакте», выявили слабые места российских властей. Удары также нанесли ущерб системам, используемым для распространения дезинформации.
В частности, после атак на дата-центры компании Yandex, которую часто сравнивают с Google, трафик компании сократился на 94%. Из-за этого пользователи столкнулись с массовыми перебоями в работе электронной почты, поисковых систем, навигации, музыкальных платформ, сервисов вызова такси, торговых площадок и финансовых услуг.
Президент Украины Владимир Зеленский заявлял, что удары по российским дата-центрам стали ответом на атаки РФ на украинские объекты. По его словам, Украина способна наносить такие же удары и отвечает на действия России зеркально.

title: Росія ввечері і вночі атакувала Київ балістикою: загиблий, пошкоджені Південний міст, гуртожиток, метро і лікарня
content_c:
Росія ввечері і вночі атакувала Київ балістикою: загиблий, пошкоджені Південний міст, гуртожиток, метро і лікарня
  - Author, Відділ новин
  - Role, ВВС News Україна
- Published
- Час прочитання: 2 хв
Ввечері 26 жовтня і вночі проти 27-го Росія атакувала Київ балістичними ракетами кількома хвилями. Вже відомо про пошкодження гуртожитку університету, лікарні та станції метро. Також є пошкодження Південного мосту.
Щонайменше одна людина загинула, ще десятеро поранені. У місті почались аварійні вимкнення світла.
Перед десятою годиною вечора Повітряні сили повідомили про балістичну атаку на столицю, ракети почали падати на Київ за кілька хвилин після оголошення тривоги.
Монітори вказують про удар близько 6-8 балістичних ракет С-400.
Перший удар прийшовся по лівобережних районах Києва.
Після 3 ночі була друга хвиля ракет, під час якої пошкодило Південний міст та адміністративну будівлю в Подільському районі.
Ввечері, за даними мерії, у Дніпровському районі біля одного з супермаркетів загинула людина.
Загалом уже відомо про 10 поранених, 9 з них госпіталізували, троє перебувають у тяжкому стані.
"Більшість із поранених - студенти з гуртожитку одного з університетів", - каже мер Віталій Кличко.
Під обстріл потрапила бригада медиків швидкої, які прямували на виклик.
Унаслідок обстрілу пошкоджений один з медичних закладів в Дніпровському районі, каже мерія. Вибуховою хвилею повибивало вікна в реанімаційному відділенні.
У Деснянському районі, попередньо, є влучання біля однієї зі станцій метро. У мережі вже є відео пошкодженої станції метро "Лісова".
У цьому ж районі є влучання біля житлового будинку, в ньому, попередньо, можуть бути заблоковані люди.
Також у Деснянському районі є влучання біля корпусів і гуртожитку одного з університетів - вже відомо, що це Державний торгівельно-економічний університет. У будівлі гуртожитку повибивало вікна.
Рух Південним мостом обмежений.
Метро на червоній лінії курсуватиме тільки до Чернігівської, а на зеленій не їздитиме на лівий берег.

Зараз ще поки не відомо точно, скільки людей постраждали. Але, на жаль, є жертви. Є поранені. Тривають рятувальні роботи. Багато пошкоджень, є інформація і про те, що люди можуть бути під завалами", - повідомив Володимир Зеленський.
Він нагадав, що затримки із постачанням протиракет для ППО допомагають російському терору по містах.
Зараз Україна не практично немає протиракет до систем PATRIOT, які єдині можуть збивати балістичні ракети.
Зеленський ввечері сказав, що найближчим часом можуть бути повторні удари. Вони стали уночі.

  - Author, Відділ новин
  - Role, ВВС News Україна
- Published
- Час прочитання: 2 хв

Щонайменше одна людина загинула, ще десятеро поранені. У місті почались аварійні вимкнення світла.
Перед десятою годиною вечора Повітряні сили повідомили про балістичну атаку на столицю, ракети почали падати на Київ за кілька хвилин після оголошення тривоги.
Монітори вказують про удар близько 6-8 балістичних ракет С-400.

title: Нічний російський обстріл знищив офіс виробника косметики Nika Zemlyanikina на десятки тисяч доларів
content_c:
Унаслідок нічної російської повітряної атаки повністю зруйновано офіс українського виробника косметики та продукції для манікюру Nika Zemlyanikina разом з обладнанням та технікою, збитки оцінюються у десятки тисяч доларів США, повідомила засновниця бренду та міжнародна інструкторка Ніка Землянікіна у Facebook.
"На щастя, всі наші люди цілі. Але офісу немає. А з ним техніки, обладнання... Вся техніка згоріла, десятки тисяч доларів втрат... Склад знаходиться в іншому місці і продукти цілі. Для покупців все буде працювати в штатному режимі", – написала підприємиця на своїй сторінці у фейсбуці.
За словами власниці бізнесу, від будівлі, де розміщувався офіс компанії, залишилися руїни, проте завдяки нічному часу удару працівниці команди були відсутні в приміщенні та уникнули поранень. Водночас оскільки складські потужності підприємства розташовані на іншій локації, вся готова продукція вціліла, що дає змогу компанії продовжувати обслуговування клієнтів у звичайному режимі.
Як повідомлялося, у ніч на вівторок та ввечері в понеділок війська РФ завдали масованого комбінованого удару по Києву та інших регіонах України. У столиці зафіксовані влучання в адміністративну будівлю та дві нежитлові споруди в Подільському районі, пошкодження інфраструктури метрополітену на Південному мосту, а також руйнування на території кампусу одного з університетів, у парку "Кіото", житлових будинках і школі в Деснянському районі, внаслідок чого одна людина загинула і 14 осіб дістали поранення.

title: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
content_c:
Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
- Published
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting.
Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy".
Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election.
Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same.
But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed.
Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias.
But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason.
Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to miss out.
The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques – appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race.
The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies - 4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult to challenge.
The result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.
But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.
Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989.
Bolsonaro had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable".
As his disconsolate supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate.
"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker told supporters. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."
After pulling off this victory, Lula faces big hurdles: a divided country, an opponent that won't recognise the result, and a hostile Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies.
Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans.
- Lula wins in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country 
  - Published1 day ago
- How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again 
  - Published18 hours ago
Reacting to the result, US President Donald Trump suggested the election had been stolen.
"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," he told reporters on Monday, without providing evidence or more details. "It looked very bad to me."
Other world leaders from across the political spectrum have congratulated Lula. Mexico's left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum said in a post on X: "The people of Brazil won."
Peru's right-wing President Keiko Fujimori praised Brazil's "democratic day". Similar messages were shared by the presidents of Chile and Ecuador.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted that their two countries had already "flourished under our partnership".
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory".
French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".
In a video posted on Instagram later on Monday, Flávio Bolsonaro said police had told him to hand over his passports and had been banned from leaving the country.
Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from the US president.
Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.

title: Chris Mason: The Budget is imminent as tricky things pile up for Burnham
content_c:
Chris Mason: The Budget is imminent as tricky things pile up for Burnham
- Published
This feels like the week where the rubber hits the road for the prime minister's new government.
It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet.
Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge.
Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into.
First up, the Budget
You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week.
There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand.
But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved in assembling this Budget that it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing.
Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years.
Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday.
You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long.
Next, Brexit – and our relationship with the EU
In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.
Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.
Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.
On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum.
Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that, instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.
Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate.
While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise.
- Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm 
  - Published1 day ago
- No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion 
  - Published12 hours ago
Some Labour MPs representing seats in the north of England and Midlands, which backed Brexit, are privately nervous about anything coming across as too enthusiastic an embrace of Brussels. A nod to that scepticism appeared to come publicly from Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood who noted that a call for an honest discussion is "not the same as settled policy".
She added: "The prime minister has also observed that there were very significant issues with freedom of movement when we were within the EU. An honest debate means actually being honest about all of the aspects of that debate and not cherry-picking."
Next month, there will be a UK-EU Summit in Brussels, which was due to happen in the summer but was postponed when Sir Keir Starmer resigned.
We can expect both sides to talk up tweaks to the current deal and the government to also, in time, set out options for what the long term relationship might look like.
On the detail, there are divisions from the cabinet and down. The key thing will be what the party decides to include or not in its next general election manifesto.
The question of North Sea oil
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East.
The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.
But what about the Rosebank field, 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil?
Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should.
It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it.
His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future."
Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw.
Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels?
Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government – which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see.
There is more: benefits, immigration, defence
Expected before long, the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn's review into young people and work – and with it a set of suggestions to try to cut the number of young people not in work, education or training and, in time, to try to cut the benefits bill too.
Plenty of Labour MPs acknowledge these are nettles that need grabbing, but how many may flinch when presented with the sharper edges of what might be proposed?
Meanwhile, we await where the government eventually ends up on how long migrants should have to wait to claim permanent residence in the UK.
And then, beyond what is set out in the Budget, how ministers will find the money to spend 3% of national income on defence by the end of the decade – and with what trade offs to make that happen.
There will be plenty to observe in the second 100 days of Burnham's government and beyond.

Chris Mason: The Budget is imminent as tricky things pile up for Burnham
- Published
This feels like the week where the rubber hits the road for the prime minister's new government.
It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet.
Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge.
Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into.
First up, the Budget
You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week.
There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand.
But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved in assembling this Budget that it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing.
Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years.
Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday.
You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long.
Next, Brexit – and our relationship with the EU
In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.
Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.
Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.
On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum.
Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that, instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.
Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate.
While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise.

- No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion 
  - Published12 hours ago

A nod to that scepticism appeared to come publicly from Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood who noted that a call for an honest discussion is "not the same as settled policy".
She added: "The prime minister has also observed that there were very significant issues with freedom of movement when we were within the EU. An honest debate means actually being honest about all of the aspects of that debate and not cherry-picking."
Next month, there will be a UK-EU Summit in Brussels, which was due to happen in the summer but was postponed when Sir Keir Starmer resigned.
We can expect both sides to talk up tweaks to the current deal and the government to also, in time, set out options for what the long term relationship might look like.
On the detail, there are divisions from the cabinet and down. The key thing will be what the party decides to include or not in its next general election manifesto.

title: 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40.' What do you want from the Budget?
content_c:
'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40.' What do you want from the Budget?
- Published
Chancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.
Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".
BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.
If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice.
Chloe's biggest worry is the cost of living. Her husband passed away four years ago and she's bringing up their 16-year-old son alone.
She's very grateful the rent for her south London maisonette is subsidised through a housing association, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."
Her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.
"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."
Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.
But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.
Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.
"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."
'I earn £22,000. Saving for a house is impossible'
Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.
Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.
"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."
Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.
He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently.
He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."
- What is the Budget and what could be in it? 
  - Published1 day ago
'I get £338 UC per month. I'm trying my best'
Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.
The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.
"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."
She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee, external scheme extended.
The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.
She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."
'I earn £30,000 and dread filling up my car'
Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.
He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.
He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."
The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.
"The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."
The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."
'I earn £150,000 and would be happy to pay more tax'
Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.
His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.
"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."
More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors.
"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."
'I have a £15,000 pension. I'm spending more of my savings'
Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her.
"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."
Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look at removing standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.
She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit, external, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.
She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".
Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".
Get in touch
What are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?
  - Published19 hours ago
  - Published3 days ago

title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
content_c:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

title: Shabana Mahmood launches review into murder of student Henry Nowak
content_c:
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak.
It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons.
Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse.
In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”
Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes.
Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak.
The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident.
Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said the review would be led by the former Conservative lord chancellor Alex Chalk KC and would report its initial findings within five months.
“Last December, Henry Nowak’s life was cut short in a horrific and senseless act of violence. My thoughts today are with Henry’s family and his friends, who have shown extraordinary courage and dignity,” she said.
“It [the review] will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene.
“It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been.
“Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct [IOPC] has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.”
Two officers, who were the first to arrive on the scene, are being investigated by the IOPC for potential gross misconduct.
The investigation is looking at why they did not recognise that Nowak needed urgent medical attention and at the decision to arrest him rather than provide first aid.
Nowak’s family welcomed the review as a “significant moment” in their fight for justice.
“Since Henry was murdered, we’ve fought tirelessly for answers to questions no family should ever have to ask. The emotional toll of that fight, on top of the unimaginable grief of losing Henry, has been immense,” the family said.

content:
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak.
It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons.
Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse.
In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”
Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes.
Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak.
The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident.
Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said the review would be led by the former Conservative lord chancellor Alex Chalk KC and would report its initial findings within five months.
“Last December, Henry Nowak’s life was cut short in a horrific and senseless act of violence. My thoughts today are with Henry’s family and his friends, who have shown extraordinary courage and dignity,” she said.
“It [the review] will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene.
“It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been.
“Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct [IOPC] has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.”
Two officers, who were the first to arrive on the scene, are being investigated by the IOPC for potential gross misconduct.
The investigation is looking at why they did not recognise that Nowak needed urgent medical attention and at the decision to arrest him rather than provide first aid.
Nowak’s family welcomed the review as a “significant moment” in their fight for justice.

title: Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
content_c:
Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
Published October 25, 2026last updated October 27, 2026
What you need to know
- Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro
- 
	It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed
- 
	In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race
- 
	Bolsonaro refused to concede, but his party recognizes Lula's victory
- 
	Trading was suspended on the stock market for half an hour on Monday morning as shares and Brazil's real currency tumbled
- 
	Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win
- 
	Germany's Merz said he looks forward to 'deepening strategic ties' with Brazil
- 
	US President Trump said the vote 'looked terrible,' but added, 'I like Lula'
This blog is now closed.
Keep reading for developments from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25, with continued coverage into Monday, October 26.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Thank you for reading
Thank you or obrigado for following our live news blog coverage of the Brazilian presidential election runoff.
We're sure to have more coverage of Brazilian politics, Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro in the coming days and weeks.
Stay tuned for more with DW.
Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula's election victory
Brazil's Liberal Party has acknowledged President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's election victory, breaking with its own candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede defeat.
"We recognize the presidential election results," party leader Valdemar Costa Neto said in a statement on Monday. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."
The statement marks a clear break with Bolsonaro's position. The senator has vowed to seek the annulment of Sunday's runoff result, claiming that a two-hour extension of voting favored Lula.
The extension was ordered due to transport problems in several cities that made it difficult for voters to reach polling stations. Bolsonaro's own campaign had also requested more voting time in some regions because of heavy rainfall.
According to electoral officials, the extension did not change the outcome of the election.
Bolsonaro has yet to publicly respond to his party's statement.
Flavio Bolsonaro says he is banned from leaving Brazil after election defeat
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro says he has been ordered to surrender his passports and is banned from leaving the country.
The right-wing senator said federal police approached him after he visited his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.
He called the move "a clear attempt to intimidate me" and claimed the order came from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Neither the court nor federal police immediately confirmed the reported ruling.
Bolsonaro said the decision was based on comments by his brother Eduardo, who had suggested he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. He denied having any plans to flee the country and said he would comply with the order.
Trump says Brazil vote 'looked terrible to me' but adds, 'I like Lula'
Ask, and you shall receive — sometimes anyway! Now a senior US government representative has commented on Brazil's vote.
Leaving Washington for a midterm election campaign rally, President Donald Trump told reporters that it "looked terrible" to him.
"I didn't take sides but it looked like another rigged election frankly... it looked so corrupt, so terrible," he said.
Asked by a reporter if he wanted to "do something about the election," Trump seemed to suggest he did not, albeit repeating his criticism of the mechanics of the vote.
"Well, I'm not running Brazil. I'm running the USA. I just thought that the election was, uh — I like Lula, I get along with him very well — I just think it had a very bad look, the election. The way it was tabulated, you know? The extension given was very strange."
US yet to comment on Brazil election
As of 3:20 p.m. in Washington D.C. (1920 GMT), the upper echelons of US government were yet to respond to the election in Brazil on Sunday.
The only October 26 State Department press releases concerned Austria's national day and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's planned trip to Georgia later in the week for a G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting.
Rubio had not opined on his social media channels and US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account — which only tends to pick up on stories with a tape delay unless they involve Trump directly — had remained inactive since Sunday night.
Lula and his Workers' Party often had strained relations with US governments, especially Republican ones, but this has been particularly pronounced in Trump's case.
Recap — Why is Bolsonaro crying foul after the voting extension?
Just joining us and wondering how Brazil's runoff vote had a considerably clearer margin of victory than predicted and yet still ended in controversy and the losing candidate refusing to concede defeat?
Challenger Flavio Bolsonaro's objections were focused around the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.
The decisions by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice on Sunday followed a complaint over allegations of pro-Bolsonaro mayors being behind public transport irregularities that may have hampered people's plans to vote.
On election night, Bolsonaro then told journalists it was "impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded."
For now it's unclear whether, as the dust settles, Bolsonaro will continue to resist the outcome and try to encourage protests in the way his now-jailed father Jair Bolsonaro did four years ago.
But two factors in particular seem to speak against the prospects of a potential Bolsonaro challenge.
Firstly, his fairly sizeable margin of defeat — losing by slightly more than 4 million votes rather than just a few thousand — makes it much more unlikely that a two-hour extension at polling stations could have even the theoretical potential of swaying the result.
And beyond that, his camp appealed for and successfully secured permission to keep polling stations open in some of Bolsonaro's southern strongholds, after torrential rains interfered with would-be voters' travel plans.
African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'
Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was one of several African leaders to congratulate Lula on Monday, saying that his renewed mandate offered an opportunity to strengthen bilateral ties.
"As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order," Tinubu said online, saying he looked forward to expanding cooperation in a raft of areas.
Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu also extended her "sincere congratulations" to Lula.
"Tanzania values its longstanding friendship with Brazil, and looks forward to continue building on this foundation to further strengthen bilateral relations and deepen cooperation, for the mutual benefit of our two nations," Suluhu said.
Seychelles President Patrick Herminie called the runoff election result "a powerful affirmation of the trust the Brazilian people have placed in President Lula's leadership," in comments published by his office online.
He said Lula's win was "a testament to his lifelong commitment to the dignity and well-being of ordinary men and women," saying the Seychelles shared Lula's values like "social justice, equality of opportunity, the protection of workers and the most vulnerable, and a model of development that places people at its center."
Herminie expressed a desire to deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in tackling climate change, protecting the oceans and advancing the interests of the Global South.
Putin congratulates Lula, praising his 'personal contribution' to bilateral ties
Russian President Vladimir Putin offered congratulations to Lula in a telegram published by the Kremlin on Monday.
"It is difficult to overstate your personal contribution to strengthening the strategic partnership between Brazil and Russia," the telegram stated.
Putin, a leader of a fellow BRICS alliance member, is one of few world leaders to have worked with Lula across all of his presidential terms, starting in 2003.
Putin also congratulated Lula on his upcoming 81st birthday, which falls on Tuesday.
The Russian president's spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow earlier in the day that the Kremlin welcomed Lula's re-election.
WATCH: Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a historic fourth term after defeating far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.
It's a historic political comeback for Lula who trailed in the first round.
DW reports from Rio de Janeiro.
Sao Paulo stock exchange halts trading over sharp drop after Lula win
Trading on the Sao Paulo stock exchange, the largest in Latin America, was suspended for 30 minutes on Monday after plummeting nearly 17% in the wake of the re-election of left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who defeated conservative Flavio Bolsonaro.
The sharp drop in the benchmark Ibovespa index triggered a 30-minute "circuit breaker" mechanism provided for "periods of sharp market decline," according to a stock exchange statement.
Meanwhile, the US dollar surged 12% against Brazil's currency, one of the real's biggest daily moves on record.
Prices of raw sugar, one of Brazil's most important exports, slid nearly 5% on the collapsing exchange rate.
Prediction markets had indicated a Bolsonaro win but the right-wing senator's refusal to concede defeat and his pledge to challenge the election result have added to investor uncertainty.
"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result, or at least allows the constitution to run its course," Chris Turner, a strategist at ING in London, told the Reuters news agency as attention turned to Lula's choice of finance minister — a clue as to his fiscal approach.
"The key signal for markets will be the next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Graham Stock told Reuters.
Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
 
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.
Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close
Here's a DW infographic on where the results stand:
France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory
Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."
French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."
"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.
"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.

title: Muss Facebook rechtswidrige Memes aufspüren?
content_c:
Klage von Renate Künast Muss Facebook rechtswidrige Memes aufspüren?
Über Social-Media-Accounts wurden Posts verbreitet, die der Grünen-Politikerin Künast falsche Zitate untergeschoben haben. Daraufhin verklagte Künast den Facebook-Betreiber Meta. Heute verhandelt der Bundesgerichtshof erneut.
Vor dem BGH in Karlsruhe geht es um ein Meme, also eine Bild-Text-Kombination, die auf Facebook weiterverbreitet wurde. Bereits 2015 tauchte dort ein Bild der Grünen-Politikerin Renate Künast auf. Dazu der Satz: "Integration fängt damit an, dass Sie als Deutscher türkisch lernen!"
Dieses angebliche Zitat von Künast war allerdings frei erfunden - eine Falschinformation, wie sie auf Facebook und anderen Sozialen Netzwerken in unüberschaubarer Zahl vorkommt, um eine Person zu verunglimpfen bzw. in ein falsches Licht zu rücken. Künast meldete das Meme, Facebook entfernte es. Das Problem war nur: Das Künast-Meme mit dem Falschzitat tauchte immer wieder in zahlreichen Varianten auf, oft mit zusätzlichen Beleidigungen gegen die Politikerin.
Klage gegen Meta
Renate Künast verklagte daraufhin den Facebook-Mutterkonzern Meta. Sie meint: Facebook müsse nicht nur die ursprüngliche Falschinformationen, sondern auch alle sinngleichen Varianten eines Postings ausfindig machen und löschen.
Meta hält dem entgegen, dass Facebook nur die konkreten Falschzitate löschen müsse, auf die es hingewiesen werde. Eine Einzelfallsuche durch Mitarbeiter sei dagegen zu aufwendig. Für eine Einzelfall-Suche sei eine manuelle Prüfung der Beiträge auf ihren Sinngehalt nötig. Dazu sei Meta als sogenannter Hosting-Anbieter aber nicht verpflichtet.
EuGH-Urteil stärkt Betroffenenrechte
Es geht also um die Frage, ob Plattformbetreiber sozialer Medien inhaltsgleiche Fake-News-Posts nach einmaliger Meldung proaktiv ausfindig machen müssen - um sie dann zu löschen. In den Vorinstanzen hatte Künast weitgehend Erfolg. Der Bundesgerichtshof als letztinstanzliches Zivilgericht setzte das Verfahren allerdings aus, um ein wichtiges Urteil des Europäischen Gerichtshofs abzuwarten.
Dieses liegt seit Dezember 2025 vor. Damals entschied der EuGH in einem anderen Fall, dass ein Plattformbetreiber geeignete Maßnahmen treffen muss, damit rechtswidrig verbreitete Inhalte nicht einfach kopiert und auf anderen Webseiten veröffentlicht werden. Der BGH muss nun entscheiden, welche Konsequenzen sich im Fall von Renate Künast daraus ergeben.

title: Wahlen in Israel: Netanjahu, Eisenkot und die Suche nach Identität
content_c:
Wahlen in Israel: Netanjahu, Eisenkot und die Suche nach Identität
27. Oktober 2026
Sie sind nicht zu übersehen: Wer mit dem Zug in die Außenbezirke der westisraelischen Stadt Sderot kommt, blickt auf riesige Wahlplakate.
Vor den Wahlen an diesem Dienstag in Israel werben sie mit eindringlichen Slogans, unter anderem für den rechtsgerichteten Likud und die rechtsextreme Partei Otzma Yehudit.
Ein Plakat ist jedoch häufiger zu sehen als alle anderen: das der liberalen Partei Jaschar von dem ehemaligen Generalstabschef der israelischen Armee Gadi Eisenkot.
Ihr Slogan "Rosh Memshala Dialna" verbindet den hebräischen Begriff für "Ministerpräsident" mit den marokkanisch-arabischen Worten für "einer von uns".
Und es gibt einen guten Grund dafür, dass sich Eisenkots Wahlkampf in Sderot und anderen Städten an Israels sozioökonomischer und politischer Peripherie auf seine marokkanischen Wurzeln konzentriert.
Sderot, Heimat marokkanisch-jüdischer Kultur
Sderot liegt in der Wüste Negev, etwa 75 Kilometer südlich von Tel Aviv und nur rund einen Kilometer von der Grenze zum Gazastreifen entfernt. In der Stadt gibt es eine große Community marokkanischer Juden.
In den vergangenen Jahrzehnten ist Sderot zu einem Symbol der marokkanisch-jüdischen Kultur in Israel geworden, die sich in Musik, Film und auch in der Staatspolitik widerspiegelt.
Historisch gilt Sderot als Hochburg der israelischen Rechten und insbesondere als eine Bastion des Likud von Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanjahu. Bei der Wahl 2022 erhielt die Partei dort mehr als 40 Prozent der Stimmen, verglichen mit 23 Prozent landesweit.
Europäische oder nordafrikanische Herkunft?
Dieses Muster spiegelt tiefere historische Spaltungen innerhalb Israels wider: zwischen den Aschkenasim, also Juden europäischer Herkunft, und den Misrachim, Juden mit Wurzeln vor allem im Nahen Osten und in Nordafrika.
Schätzungen zufolge ist etwa die Hälfte der jüdischen Bevölkerung Israels misrachischer Herkunft, was rund vier Millionen Menschen entspricht.
Misrachische Juden waren seit den frühen Jahren des israelischen Staates häufig Diskriminierung und Vernachlässigung ausgesetzt. Diese Ungleichheiten prägen bis heute die wirtschaftliche und soziale Realität Israels sowie den politischen Diskurs.
Eisenkot: Bekenntnis zur marokkanischen Herkunft
Doch in diesem Wahlkampf erhält dieses Thema besondere Aufmerksamkeit. Gadi Eisenkot, Netanjahus wichtigster Herausforderer, ist marokkanischer Herkunft und wuchs in Eilat auf, einer Stadt mit einer großen nordafrikanisch-jüdischen Bevölkerung.
Eisenkots Partei Jaschar warf dem Likud vor, seine misrachischen Politiker an den Rand zu drängen. Mit dem Wahlslogan "Netanjahu: Lasst die Misrachim Interviews geben", machte die Partei auf dieses Versäumnis aufmerksam.
Im Live-Fernsehen behauptete der rechtsgerichtete Journalist Yinon Magal, einer der lautstärksten Unterstützer Netanjahus, Eisenkot werde von einer elitären aschkenasischen Gruppe kontrolliert, und bezeichnete ihn als "Affen". Netanjahu, der europäischer Herkunft ist, verurteilte diese Äußerung.
Doppelte Identität und Diskriminierung
Der in Marokko geborene Daniel Ben-Simon, ein preisgekrönter israelischer Journalist und ehemaliger Abgeordneter, sagte der Deutschen Welle, dass Eisenkots öffentliche Betonung seiner Herkunft möglicherweise durch Magals Äußerungen ausgelöst worden sei. Gleichwohl habe sie eine wichtige historische Bedeutung.
"Die Menschen verwenden Begriffe wie 'Dialna' normalerweise nicht mit Stolz", sagte Ben-Simon mit Blick auf Eisenkots Verwendung des arabischen Ausdrucks für "einer von uns" auf seinen Wahlplakaten. Die israelische Gesellschaft habe lange versucht, die arabischen Identitäten nordafrikanischer Juden zu verdrängen.
"Durch die Verwendung eines solchen Begriffs schafft man eine neue Identität: eine israelisch-marokkanische Identität", so Ben-Simon. "Eisenkot ist der Erste, der es ermöglicht, diese doppelte Identität offen auszudrücken und sich dabei dennoch vollständig zu Hause zu fühlen."
Israels historische Spaltung
Nach der Gründung Israels 1948 verfolgte die regierende sozialistische Partei Mapai, deren Führung überwiegend aus Aschkenasim bestand, eine diskriminierende Politik gegenüber den Mizrachim. Von den Mizrachim wurde häufig erwartet, sich zu "europäisieren", anstatt ihre eigene Kultur, ihr Erbe oder die arabische Sprache zu bewahren.
Diese Ungleichheiten hatten auch eine materielle Dimension. In den ersten Jahrzehnten des Staates erhielten europäische Einwanderer oft bessere Wohnungen und Arbeitsplätze, während viele Juden aus arabischsprachigen Ländern in sogenannte Ma'abarot (Übergangslager) geschickt wurden.
Diese befanden sich häufig in abgelegenen Regionen mit mangelhafter Infrastruktur. Viele dieser Lager entwickelten sich später zu sogenannten Entwicklungsstädten, die im Vergleich zu den zentralen Regionen Israels dauerhaft unterfinanziert blieben.
Mizrachim unterstützen Likud
Dies führte wiederum zu weit verbreiteter Armut. Sderot im Süden des Landes ist eine der bekanntesten dieser Entwicklungsstädte.
Für viele Mizrachim symbolisierte der eingeschränkte Zugang zu Arbeitsplätzen, Bildung und Infrastruktur die langjährige Ausgrenzung durch das politische Establishment.
Der Likud, der 1973 als rechtsgerichtetes Parteienbündnis gegründet wurde, nutzte diese Unzufriedenheit geschickt für sich. So trug die Unterstützung der Mizrachim für die Partei bei den Wahlen 1977 maßgeblich zum Sieg des Likud bei.
Seitdem werden Mizrachim häufig mit dem Likud in Verbindung gebracht, obwohl die Partei bislang nie einen Parteivorsitzenden mizrachischer Herkunft hatte.
Sderot: Hamas greift immer wieder an
In den vergangenen zwei Jahrzehntenwar Sderot aufgrund seiner Nähe zum Gazastreifen immer wieder Ziel von Raketenangriffen der militanten Hamas. Während des von der Hamas angeführten Terrorangriffs vom 7. Oktober 2023 wurde die Stadt besonders schwer getroffen. Mehr als 50 Menschen kamen dabei ums Leben.
Seit seit dem Angriff vor drei Jahren ist die Einwohnerzahl der Stadt um rund 5.000 Menschen auf etwa 40.000 Einwohner gestiegen. Viele junge Familien haben sich dort niedergelassen, sowohl aus ideologischer Überzeugung als auch aufgrund staatlicher Förderprogramme.
Bei einem Spaziergang durch die Stadt fällt auf, dass die sogenannte nationalreligiöse Gemeinschaft zunehmend an Einfluss gewinnt. Diese Bevölkerungsgruppe unterstützt in der Regel die rechtsextreme Partei Religiöser Zionismus von Bezalel Smotrich.
Smotrich gehört zu den wichtigsten Partnern in Netanjahus Regierungskoalition. Zwar stärken Stimmen für Smotrich und seine Partei faktisch das politische Lager Netanjahus, dennoch könnte die Likud-Partei des Ministerpräsidenten selbst in Sderot Stimmenverluste hinnehmen müssen.
Unabhängig vom Ausgang der Wahl dürfte sich die Wahrnehmung Sderots als Stadt der marokkanisch-stämmigen Juden vorerst kaum verändern. Ein Wahlsieg Eisenkots könnte eine Gelegenheit sein, die zukünftige Identität marokkanischer Juden in Israel neu zu definieren, meint Daniel Ben-Simon.
Dieser Artikel wurde aus dem Englischen adaptiert.
description: Eisenkot gegen Netanjahu, marokkanische Herkunft gegen europäische Abstammung: Bei den Wahlen in Israel fordert ein Ex-General den Premier heraus. Es geht nicht nur um rechts oder links, sondern um nationale Identität.

title: Після нічної атаки балістикою РФ зранку запустила нові цілі: які області під загрозою (мапа)
content_c:
Після нічної атаки балістикою РФ зранку запустила нові цілі: які області під загрозою (мапа)
Українців закликають не ігнорувати сигнали повітряної тривоги та перебувати в укриттях до відбою.
Вночі проти 27 жовтня росіяни вдарили по Україні балістикою, але на ранок зберігається загроза повітряних атак. У кількох регіонах оголошено повітряну тривогу.
Що відомо про російську атаку — читайте у матеріалі ТСН.ua.
Повітряні сили ЗСУ попередили про активність тактичної авіації РФ на північно-східному напрямку та небезпеку застосування авіаційних засобів ураження по прифронтових областях.
Окрім того, існує загроза БпЛА і КАБів. Так, на Полтавщині зафіксували реактивний безпілотник, який пролітав повз Кобеляки курсом на Кременчук. Водночас на півночі Харківщини зафіксували загрозу застосування керованих авіаційних бомб (КАБів).

title: Рейтинг одобрения Трампа несколько вырос накануне промежуточных выборов в США — опрос Reuters/Ipsos
content_c:
Рейтинг одобрения президента США Дональда Трампа вырос до 32% с рекордно низкого уровня (31%), зафиксированного на прошлой неделе, накануне промежуточных выборов 3 ноября, которые определят, какая партия будет контролировать Конгресс, согласно опросу Reuters/Ipsos.
Республиканцы Трампа борются за сохранение большинства партии в Палате представителей и Сенате. Новый опрос показал, что зарегистрированные избиратели в целом отдавали предпочтение демократам перед республиканцами (47% против 36%), когда их спрашивали, за какую партию они проголосовали бы на выборах в Конгресс (без указания конкретного кандидата). 11% опрошенных заявили, что не знают, за кого бы проголосовали, если бы выборы состоялись сегодня.
Разрыв в 11% между демократами и республиканцами на 1% меньше, чем в опросе Reuters/Ipsos, проведенном на прошлой неделе. В новом опросе избирателей, которые еще не определились, дополнительно спросили о том, к какой партии они склоняются. С учётом их ответов общенациональная гонка выглядит ещё более напряжённой: демократы лидируют с преимуществом в 9% — 50% против 41%.
Для республиканцев потеря контроля над любой из палат Конгресса может затруднить реализацию программы Трампа в последние два года его второго президентского срока.
Хотя такие опросы дают представление о настроениях общественности на национальном уровне, они не отражают нюансов предвыборной гонки в отдельных штатах и округах — борьбы, в которой республиканцы обладают определенными структурными преимуществами.
Демократам будет сложно завоевать большинство в Сенате
Политические аналитики в целом считают, что у демократов есть хорошие шансы получить контроль над Палатой представителей, но партии придется приложить больше усилий, чтобы победить в Сенате.
Пока неизвестно, сколько избирателей на самом деле придут на избирательные участки. Среди избирателей, которые, скорее всего, будут голосовать, демократы опережают республиканцев на 9% — 53% против 44%.
Похоже, что борьба за Конгресс вращается вокруг взглядов на инфляцию, которая резко выросла после того, как в феврале Трамп начал наносить удары по Ирану, что привело к росту цен на бензин. 73% избирателей заявили, что ситуация со стоимостью жизни ухудшается.
До начала войны с Ираном опросы Reuters/Ipsos показывали, что избиратели отдают предпочтение республиканцам перед демократами как лучшим распорядителям экономики. Согласно новому опросу, 37% избирателей считают, что у демократов лучший подход к экономике, по сравнению с 33%, которые в этом вопросе отдали предпочтение республиканцам.
Опрос также показал, что избиратели-демократы более активно настроены на участие в голосовании: 46% демократов заявили, что они “с нетерпением ждут промежуточных выборов”, по сравнению с 30% республиканцев, высказавших такое же мнение.
Опрос Reuters/Ipsos проводился в онлайн-режиме и охватил 1679 взрослых американцев, в том числе 1280 зарегистрированных избирателей. Погрешность составляет 2% для всех взрослых респондентов и 3% для зарегистрированных избирателей.
Бывший посол Украины в США Валерий Чалый в статье "Куда движется Америка Трампа: три сценария промежуточных выборов в США" писал, что Трамп может утратить абсолютную власть в Соединенных Штатах, поскольку Конгресс "выскальзывает" из рук республиканцев. Дипломат считает наиболее вероятным “традиционный сценарий” после промежуточных выборов, который предусматривает победу демократов в Палате представителей и сохранение контроля республиканцев над Сенатом. В таких условиях влияние Белого дома и лично Трампа может уменьшиться, но при этом сохранятся возможности блокировать инициативы демократов через Сенат и президентское вето.
description: Потеря республиканцами контроля над любой из палат Конгресса затруднила бы реализацию программы Трампа в последние два года его президентства.

title: Київський метрополітен відновив рух червоною гілкою і тимчасово зупинив поїзди частиною зеленої після обстрілу – Кличко
content_c:
Київський метрополітен у вівторок уранці повністю відновив рух поїздів червоною лінією після усунення наслідків вечірнього російського обстрілу і водночас тимчасово призупинив сполучення між станціями "Осокорки" та "Червоний хутір" на зеленій гілці через пошкодження інфраструктури на Південному мосту, повідомив міський голова столиці Віталій Кличко у вівторок вранці.
"Всі станції метро на червоній гілці відкриті для пасажирів. Рух поїздів здійснюється між станціями "Академмістечко" – "Лісова"... Рух же поїздів між станціями "Осокорки" – "Червоний хутір" на зеленій гілці метро тимчасово призупинений. Через влучання в інфраструктуру метро на Південному мосту", – написав Кличко у своєму у телеграм-каналі.
За словами Кличка, пізно ввечері в понеділок унаслідок ворожої атаки виникли пошкодження на ділянці між станціями "Дарниця" і "Чернігівська", а також виходів зі станції "Лісова", проте фахівці підприємства впродовж ночі виконали відновлювальні роботи для забезпечення руху всією лінією. Водночас столична влада вивела на лінії додаткові автобуси для посилення маршрутів наземного громадського транспорту, який сполучає лівий і правий береги міста.
Як повідомлялося, війська РФ у вівторок завдали удару по Південному мосту в Києві з пошкодженням розташованої на ньому інфраструктури метрополітену, а загальна кількість постраждалих у столиці внаслідок ворожих обстрілів із вечора понеділка зросла до 14 осіб при одному загиблому.

title: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
content_c:
Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
- Published
Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing.
It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.
Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.
Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse".
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip.
"Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.
This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.
Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".
His legal team has filed a motion to dismiss the charges.
Former federal prosecutor Glenn Kirschner told the BBC that the case may have exceeded the 10-year statute of limitations, giving the motion to dismiss the charges "a very good chance of being granted".
Kirschner said it seemed like the charges against Comey were a "revenge-fuelled attempt by Donald Trump to have his Department of Justice find something that might stick".
Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election.
Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so.
Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding.
He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November.
In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life.
The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president.
Comey denies any wrongdoing, saying he did not know what the numbers meant, and accusing the prosecution of political motivation. That case is ongoing.
The latest charges against Comey were made public the same day a federal judge ruled the justice department illegally fired his daughter, Maurene Comey.
Maurene Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father and because of her perceived political affiliations.
The judge ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
